description:
Invisible Earth is a team from Granada, Spain, founded by Alberto and Dani. We bring together software development, data analysis, design and research to explore new ways of understanding our planet.

For NASA Space Apps 2026, we're taking on the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge with curiosity, creativity and a shared goal: turning complex satellite data into something people can explore, understand and actually use.
summary: Invisible Earth turns NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations into an interactive 3D experience. Visitors choose a place, follow observations of the same area, and explore how the surface may have changed. A guided story, a quality layer and a timeline help make satellite radar data easier to understand. The application includes examples from Venezuela, Granada, Mexico City, Nepal and Kamchatka. It shows radar displacement along the satellite’s line of sight or changes in radar coherence, depending on the case. Animations and exaggerated relief explain the process; they are not continuous recordings. The project is intended for curious members of the public and educators, although classroom use has not yet been validated.
details:
THE CHALLENGE

Earth-observation satellites collect information about changes that are difficult to see from the ground. Radar products are powerful, but interpreting them requires context about satellite geometry, observation dates and data quality. Our goal is to make those observations easier to explore and explain.

OUR SOLUTION

Invisible Earth is a browser-based, interactive 3D application. Visitors choose a location, follow a guided sequence and explore a radar comparison on terrain. They can navigate the map, inspect a point, check signal quality and switch between available pairs of observations. The same experience can be explored step by step or in Film mode. The Point Guide preview uses prepared explanations to help visitors interpret the radar reading at a selected point.

HOW IT WORKS

We prepare NASA–ISRO NISAR geocoded unwrapped interferogram (GUNW) products distributed by ASF DAAC, together with elevation tiles. Our processing extracts areas of interest and prepares radar layers for rendering. The application combines them with terrain meshes and WebGL shaders. For Venezuela, the highlighted comparison uses observations from 13 and 25 June 2026; the 24 June earthquakes occurred between the two passes.

WHAT THE VISITOR LEARNS

Depending on the case, the application shows line-of-sight displacement or changes in radar coherence. A quality layer helps users avoid treating every coloured pixel as equally reliable. The timeline represents pairs of observations, not continuous footage. The terrain and some motion are exaggerated for visibility; radar sweeps and event animations are illustrative. If real radar data is unavailable, the application can display a labelled synthetic fallback.

WHO IT IS FOR

The experience is designed for people curious about Earth observation, including educators who might introduce radar data in class. We have not yet validated classroom use with teachers or students. Our intended impact is to make a path from satellite observations to an explorable question more approachable.

TOOLS AND RESPONSIBLE USE

We built the interface with TypeScript, Vite, Three.js and WebGL. Data preparation uses Python, earthaccess, h5py and NumPy. OpenAI Codex and ChatGPT supported development and writing. The English narration is an AI-generated synthetic voice produced with Microsoft Edge text-to-speech; its audio metadata identifies it as synthetic. The team is responsible for reviewing the work and its interpretation. We used Node.js to prepare the terrain and globe, FFmpeg to process media, and Playwright for app captures and testing. The web presentation uses Slidev, Vue.js and Google Fonts, and is hosted on Vercel.

LIMITATIONS

A single radar line of sight does not independently separate horizontal and vertical movement. Displacement maps use a reference, and low-coherence areas require caution. Processing choices, reference selection and interpretation still require independent scientific review. This is an educational prototype, not an operational emergency or hazard-assessment tool.
